speechtext:
When the House rose at six o'clock, I had had the pleasure of placing upon the records two tables of statistics, giving the trade of this country with the United States during the period of the old treaty. I stated that one of those tables was absolutely false, and that was the table which had always been used in the discussion upon the question of trade relations with the United States from the time the old reciprocity treaty was abrogated. Now, the figures of that table, which table I would call the greatest statistical lie of the nineteenth century, showed that there was a balance of trade in favour of this country for that period of $31,955,131. On the face of it, that would appear to be a good thing for Canada, because in those days we did not have that heresy proclaimed that it is a good thing for a country to have a balance of trade against it. In fact, the doctrine used to be preached by those high priests of the Liberal party, by those great financial lights of the Liberal party, that if a country did not have a trade balance in its favour sooner or later that country would go to ruin; in other words, that commodity must pay for commodity, which is a doctrine of free traders from time immemorial. I find that that false statement was the statement upon which commercial union and reciprocity were fought, and which I may say was sanctioned by the United States, which published it in its records, showing that they deliberately intended to falsify the facts, I find that according to the true statement, the actual American figures showed, during the period of the treaty, a balance in favour of the United States of $34,520,007. So the treaty was not quite so good for Canada as it appeared on the face of it.
The right hon. leader of the House took



issue with the members on this side of the House, who declared that this government and this parliament had received no mandate from the people to negotiate this treaty. The Prime Minister took exception to that statement, and said that neither was there any mandate for the old treaty, that there was no mandate for confederation, in fact, that there was no mandate for any great piece of legislation that had been passed in this country. I pointed out in the earlier portion of my speech that before the old treaty of 1854 was arranged an address was passed by the parliament of Canada on May 12, 1846, which address was forwarded to Great Britain. Negotiations followed, with the result that a' treaty was concluded in June, 1854, ratification was exchanged at Washington on September 9, 1854, it was proclaimed September 11, 1854, and took effect March 16, 1855. Now, throughout the whole period of that treaty after it was consummated by the United States, the arguments were that it would only be a very short time until Canada became a portion of the United States. Did I wish to do so, I could take an hour in placing on the ' Hansard ' extracts to show that the leading American newspapers and writers took that view of the question. The prevalent view was expressed by the ' North American Review,' which was at that time the leading exponent of public opinion in the United States. The chief writer in the review laid down the doctrine that the treaty had been given to Canada in order that Canada might be led gently into annexation.
Now, Sir, we have had some experience of attempts to force us into annexation. Pour times, by force of arms, attempts were made to bring about the annexation of Canada to the United States. Those who visit Quebec can see a bronze plate beneath the ramparts of the city showing where Montgomery fell in the first great invasion. If you go to Niagara you will find a monument erected to Sir Isaac Brock, which commemorates our deliverance from the second invasion. You will find there was an invasion in 1837, at least an indirect invasion, backed up by the United States, to bring about the independence and ultimately the annexation of this country. I am not speaking my own words in recounting these facts, because any one who reads the chief authors on Canadian history will find these facts for himself. Read McMullen, or any other historian that is recognized as an authority, and you will ascertain the facts I mention. In 1866 there was a direct invasion; that, followed the abrogation of the treaty. Now, what occurred during the existence of that treaty? The American Congress was constantly threatening to abrogate it. Early during the existence of the treaty we had Mr. CURRIE (Simcoe).
to place a tariff on the manufactures of other countries in order to raise a revenue. Mr. Galt, who was then Finance Minister, framed that tariff, and he had a very hard time of it. He had to meet the opposition of the free trade element in Canada, who were largely pro-annexationists at that time. He had to meet the opposition of the English merchants, and if you will read the history of that epoch you will find that he went over to England and expostulated with the clothing merchants of Manchester, and excused Canada, and said it was impossible for this country to get a revenue unless they put a tariff on British goods as well as goods from other countries. He had also to meet with great opposition in the United States. The American papers discussed this question, and I find in the columns of the Toronto ' Globe,' which at that period was a very good journal, extracts time after time from the American papers. The Chicago ' Journal ' was one of them; it stated that unless Canada changed her ways and took the duties off American manufactured goods coming into Canada the treaty would be abrogated. I do not wish to burden ' Hansard ' with all these details, but I merely state what took place.	-
Now, I find that as the time approached for the abrogation of that treaty, which broke up the commercial relations existing between the two countries, it was found necessary, owing to the fact that there was a small number in the Conservative party and a small number in the Liberal party who were very noisy, and continually crying out for a reciprocity treaty, and even for annexation, it was found absolutely necessary, I say, for the great chiefs _ of both parties to forai a coalition to bring about confederation. I find, also, that it was the party to which I have the honour now to belong, and which then called itself the coalition or Liberal-Conservative party, that was chiefly instrumental in bringing about confederation. That party, Sir, bore the brunt of the struggle in favour of the confederation of Canada. It fought another great battle in 1878, and it fought a battle in 1891.
Whatever fault there may be with_ our leaders, and we are all weak men and liable to make errors, the dominant note in the life and history of the Liberal-Conservative party from that date has been Canadian-ism. Not going too far pro-British-why. Sir, Sir John Macdonald, on one occasion had to say that if a certain Act of his in the way of duties on British goods was going to hurt British connection, it was so. much the worse for British connection. Again, that policy has been constantly to prevent any shifting of the position towards the United States, constantly leading along the middle path that was blazed out by

George Brown and Sir John A. Macdonald. That is the path, we are treading to-day, and that is the path you will find the young men of this country are going to follow. They are not going to follow any by-roads towards reciprocity of tariff or anything else, they stand first for Canadianism and they intend to remain Canadian. As one of the younger element it shocks me to think that gentlemen will get up in this House and plead that 50 years ago this desire was so and so, that it still remains strong, and that it is hoped to accomplish it now. I heard the Finance Minister and his colleague, the Minister of Customs speak. What was the burden of their speeches? That a duty had been laid on the Liberal party many years ago and also on the Liberal Conservative party to bring about reciprocity of trade between the United States and Canada and the Minister of Finance says: I am pleased to say I can now come into this House and say that my labours are done, I have paid my debt. It reminded me very much of the story so eloquently told by Balzac, the great French novelist, of the young couple who were married. The young man had received an appointment under the government, and they were invited to a ball. The bride was anxious to appear as handsome as possible at this official ball, and borrowed from a friend of hers a diamond necklace. Terrible to relate, at the ball, or on the way home the necklace was lost. The young couple discussed the matter and decided not to say anything about it to the friend who had lent the necklace, but to go to a jeweller's purchase a similar necklace and mortgage their whole life's work to pay off the debt. They carried out that programme. Throughout their whole lives, they starved and slaved and saved every dollar. They did not have sufficient food or clothing, and finally when they were both old and decrepit, the day came when at last they had paid their debt. And then the lady thought she would go and tell her friend the whole story. She told the whole story and her friend after hearing the story of her life work and sacrifice, informed her that the diamonds she had lent her were paste, an imitation, and that the necklace was worth only 35 francs. We have here a tragedy of a similar character. Here are two honourable gentlemen who all their lives have been slaving, struggling, labouring, saving up every copper, waiting every moment patiently for a call to come to Washington to accomplish a treaty of this kind. They come back to this House and the Minister of Finance says: The debt is paid, I have finished my work for the right hon. gentleman as he also wanted to finish his work. These hon. gentlemen are no doubt staggered and shocked to find that the country does not appreciate that sacrifice, that this House does not appreciate that tragedy, and that everybody 1514
is really laughing at them for being such fools as to go over to the United States and bring back what is in reality a pinchbeck, an imitation treaty. From the time that the first treaty was negotiated until the negotiation of this treaty there was1 not a moment when the United States would not have given concurrent legislation in this matter of trade. Why? Because they have failed four times to annex this country by force of arms. The people of this country having suffered the torch, the destruction of their homes, the death of their nearest friends and relatives, and failed to accede to the demand for annexation. The Americans had decided to adopt other methods. I am not waving any old flags, but I will try to place before the House the reason why thinking men say that this treaty will ultimately lead to annexation. I acknowledge the fact that on the face of it a person will be very much inclined to say: What harm is there to trade between these two countries; there can be no question, but it will be a benefit to both of them. That is a sensible question to me. But I find that on every occasion when an attempt was made to bring about a crisis in the commercial affaire of this country, the Americans had in view to coerce us commercially which is the method adopted by the United States so successfully to coerce other countries to come into the union. They succeeded in the case of the Sandwich islands. There is one man in the United States Congress, in the House of Representatives, Mr. Champ Clarke, who, whilst he may have the reputation from the hon. gentlemen opposite of being a humorist, has the reputation of being the best posted man in history in the whole United States. Without exception there is no man who knows the history of the operation of congressional and state government in his country better than Mr. Champ Clarke. When this matter was under discussion in the Senate of the United States, Mr. Clarke let fall one simple remark which the newspapers of this country published but which very few people recognized, as being of importance. This is what he said, speaking of this treaty:
The agricultural schedule is largely a humbug, a delusion and a snare. We had a reciprocity treaty with the Sandwich Islands, because from the first, we intended to swallow them.
Now, Sir, what are the facts of the case.
I am going_ to tell you the facts, to recite them to this House, in order to show you that there is a very strong analogy. A reciprocity treaty was made with the Sandwich islands in 1875. Sugar is one of the principal products of the Sandwich islands, and one of the principal products of the United States. There was no necessity for reciprocity in that case any more than there is

necessity for reciprocity in wheat, but a reciprocity treaty was established. The treaty was for seven years, to be abrogated on twelve months' notice, xn 1887, after a great deal of grumbling, President Cleveland said he would not grant a new treaty because he was opposed to a reciprocity treaty on principle. But he had a sudden change of mind, and granted a new treaty without any reason being given. But here was a reason of the treaty of 1887. The United States was given a harbour on the Sandwich islands known as Pearl River harbour in perpetuity. In that way they got the first small portion of land from the Sandwich islands. The treaty expired in 1891. Its abrogation was subject to one year's notice. I wish to tell the House that during all the time that that treaty was in force there was not a session of Congress in which some blustering Senator or representative did not threaten to dissolve the treaty between the United States and the Sandwich islands.
There was a continuous panic all the time in the Sandwich Islands; sugar lands [DOT]declined in value, and property generally was depressed, because they could not tell what moment their chief market would be [DOT]destroyed. Talk of analogy, is not that analogy enough. Before the McKinley Bill was passed we had a trade with the United States in barley, but when the duty was raised our farmers suffered, and there was a tremendous dislocation in trade and hard times. Well, in the Sandwich Islands reciprocity organizations were formed but the United States would not annex the Sandwich Islands off the bat because they would not honourably accept the bonded indebtedness. Their plan was to let the trouble go on, and there was a revolution, and a protectorate government was formed which disavowed largely the debt of the island, and, after the process had continued long enough to tire out the bondholders the United States quietly annexed the Sandwich Islands. We are told by writers on the subject that with the single exception of Spreckles, the Americans came over to the Sandwich Islands without a shinplaster and they were no sooner there than they married natives, grabbed all the lands and property, seized all the banks, and when the protectorate came they were in possession of the whole situation. We see in that instance a short term treaty; we see constant threats of abrogation; we see commercial coercion more successful in the Sandwich Islands than a straight war would have been. Now, let us see what, about Cuba. At one time Cuba and Porto Rico belonged to Spain, and I do not now refer to the Philippine Islands because they were conquered by force of arms. In 1891 there was an agitation in Cuba for the enlargement of the sugar market; something similar, Mr. CURRIE (Simcoe).
only stronger to the agitation xve have had for this treaty. The sugar planters and the tobacco planters had a splendid market in Britain, and all the better grades of tobacco were purchased in Europe, as they are purchased to-day, only second grades reaching the United States and Canada. The planters had a market in Great Britain but they wanted a wider market, just - as our farmers in the Northwest seem to want two markets where now they have one. At last in 1891 a reciprocity treaty was consummated between the United States and Spain, but it was not long in force before there were threats in the American Senate to abrogate it. The sugar interests in the United States were all the time looming up on the horizon, and as soon as the trade had been established by American traders and Hebrew dealers in tobacco, the question arose among the Cuban planters: are we going to lose the American market? But, agitation did not go swift enough; arms were sent from the United States to the half black natives; blacks there sent from San Domingo as workmen and were no sooner landed than they were prepared to fight, and a revolution was fomented. And what for? To bring about annexation to the United States in order, as they said, that Cuba should have a free market in the United States. The Spanish American war followed. Spain ceded Cuba to the United States, and the United States turned Cuba over to the tender mercies of a native government. Why was this done? It was because if the United States remained in possession of Cuba the foreign bondholders might have come on the scene to ask that their bonds be paid, but by turning the country over to a provisional government the debt of the country was discharged by that very act, and when the foreign bondholders are all dead and forgotten, inside of possibly ten years, Cuba will have the same destiny as the Sandwich Islands. A writer on this question, Mr. Lawrence Laughlin, of Chicago, pointing out the ultimate end of the Sandwich Islands, states that what had been foretold from the first, viz., that the reciprocity treaty would bring about annexation, had come true. Here we have two outstanding examples; _ we have a reciprocity treaty, connection is formed between the two countries of a commercial character, commercial coercion from the United States follows, and the national entity of the other country is wiped out. Now, in our own country, why did they seek confederation in 1866. I will pljce upon the records of the House an extract from the speech of a great Liberal of those days, and it is an argument against this treaty more eloquent and potent than anything I could say. I quoted from the same authority this afternoon, I quote

him again, so that his remarks may sink deep into the heart of my free trade friend from Nova Scotia. And, that reminds me of the great convention of the boards of trade of Canada and the United States held in Detroit in 1866, and at that convention speeches were made by prominent Americans in which they invited Canada to join the United States and partake of the pleasures of annexation and the free markets they could afford. There was at that convention a great Nova Scotian, Joseph Howe, and when he rose to speak on that occasion he told the Americans present how his son had gone to the United States when the civil war broke out, and how he had fought for the union, and how he had come home with an honourable discharge, and Joseph Howe said: I tell you gentlemen that if I should do anything to bring about the annexation of my country, and to haul down the British flag that floats over Canada, the very first man to blow out my brains would be my beloved son who fought so gallantly for your union. Well, Sir, we have not such Nova Scotians to-day.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Why not?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
I cannot understand why; they are largely free traders. Let me tell you something about the Nova Scotians we have to-day. Nova Scotia came into the confederation in good faith, but unfortunately for that province there has always been a free trade element among its people; a free trade element that believes in the doctrine' that what money is made by one industry must be lost by somebody else, because they cannot understand that there may be a profit at both ends of the bargain. The hon. gentleman who went to Washington to negotiate this treaty is one of these men, and I say without any hesitation whatever, that Nova Scotia with her splendid harbours, and her wealth of coal and iron, and her intelligent population, had she the proper men to lead her in her legislative halls, would be to-day greater than any state in the union, for not only would she be manufacturing goods for Canada and Canadians but she would be manufacturing goods in competition with Germany and every country in the world. But, that narrow spirit which keeps constantly agitating against the condition of things that exist, that narrow spirit has dominated Nova Scotia and its politics and it is only within recent years that successful industries have been established in Nova Scotia, and which today I am happy to say are so prosperous.
Now, let us see what confederation has done for Nova Scotia. We men in the middle west are not narrow or provincial; we are willing at all times to hold up our end d the log. and when it comes to paying the
piper, we are willing to pay our share fairly and justly. The workingmen of the province of Ontario, whose children eat the bread that is baked with soft coal, have been paying three and a quarter millions of dollars a year in coal duties-why? In order that their brethern in the coal mines of Nova Scotia might have protection and labour. They have paid three-quarters of a million dollars a year in bounties on iron and steel in order that the men who work in the iron mills of Nova Scotia might have protection and labour. Is that selfish? Have hon. members ever read a word in the newspapers of my province against that proposition? But Nova Scotia continues to send to this House, free traders, men who are constantly attacking the best interests of this country, and seeking to destroy its industries and to prevent our workingmen in the Central West from having employment, men who believe that what is good for one part of the country must be injurious to the other. If Nova Scotia continues to send such men to this House-and there is no doubt, from the signs of the times, that there will be a change in the next parliament-I for one, staunch protectionist as I am, will have to consider whether it will be worth while for the rest of the country to grant a duty of 50 cents a ton to Nova Scotia on soft coal, and a bounty on her steel in order that she may send free traders to the parliament of Canada. I think that is a fair proposition, and, I say it unreservedly, that if such a state of affairs occurs after the next election, and I belong to the dominant party, I shall be one of the men to stand up in this House, and say: No, Nova Scotia does not want protection; take the duty off her coal-she sends free traders here; Nova Scotia does not want protection on her steel-she sent here a man, a free trader, who threw the markets of Canada open to American farm products. Let Nova Scotia play fair in this matter and send men here who are more in touch with the true interests1 of Nova Scotia, not men who come and talk free trade and practice protection at the expense of the rest of the country. I hope the hon. gentleman has now heard enough about Nova Scotia. He can take that and find out if he can get elected on it in Nova Scotia after this; because he is elected by the coal -workers of that province.
There is one thing which I very much deprecate in discussions of this kind, and that is, that the tone of the discussion should be lowered to any personal note. I was deeply grieved this afternoon to- hear the right hon. gentleman who leads this House, and who happens not to be here at the present moment, state that the members of his government were great financiers.

speechtext: I do not think he did. He could mot tell us of any treaty in which there was one. I would like to hear from him so that we might test his knowledge of this treaty making clause. When a man sets about making treaties, he ought to be acquainted with the treaties of other countries. Can the hon. minister tell us off-hand of one or two in which this reciprocal form is used?

speechtext: Yes, I have evidently floored the hon. gentleman on the simple question of treaty making.

speechtext: He shall see

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
had a similar experience with the fisheries in Ontario and in Manitoba. And this government stands supine, and by its supineness enables the Americans, by their regulations, to come in, throttle our fishermen and squeeze the last drop of blood out of them. They come in and virtually take possession of our fisheries as if in fee simple, and compel our men to slave for them, paying them the price that goes to the mere hewers of wood and drawers of water, and as middle men they make enormous profits. They are the master's and we are the peon's. This is the condition that exists in our Atlantic fisheries. All this would be remedied if the government would form co-operative societies amongst our fishermen, organize our fisheries in the proper manner, put in freezers and give these men a chance to get their fish to market; and, above all, put an export duty on every pound of fish that went off the banks or out of the country except in a Canadian bottom. The application of the good old navigation law-that is what would build up this industry. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) laughs. He would not raise a hand, as did the knight in the other chamber, Sir George Ross, who, when Prime Minister of Ontario, declared to the Americans that they were not to take our logs out of our forests unless they manufactured them in this country. These men do not understand the principle of a great national policy developing industries of size and consequence.
I pass on now to other industries. I have pointed out that the strength of the nation lies in iron and steel. And all honour to the men, I say, who have established great iron and steel works in Nova Scotia- mostly western men, it is true, but also including eastern men, who have made money out of it, as we are glad to- know. So we have the example not only of the Nova Scotia iron and steel works, but of the car works, of the stove works and many others. And yet these men of the east send men to represent them in this House, a majority of them rank free traders, as I regard them.
The hon. member for Carleton, New Brunswick (Mr. Carvell) told us that it was too bad the duty should remain on shingles, and said that he was interested in a shingle mill and a lath mill.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: And in pretty nearly everything else.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
Yes, I suppose in nearly everything in the province he is interested in some way. He told us that they could get so much more for their stuff if they had the stuff on the American side. Why, let him follow the natural course of the policy of this government that he supports-move his shingle mill across the line and then ship the logs over and cut Mr. CURRIE (Simcoe).
them there. There is no string on the logs, and this exportation of logs in an unmanufactured state is the very thing that- this policy is intended to bring about from start to finish.
There are other articles on the free list, such as talc, asbestos and gypsum. There are vast deposits of gypsum in New Brunswick and around the Bras d'Or lakes in Nova Scotia-the best, possibly, in America -and some in Ontario also. Now, a strange thing about this gypsum situation is that we shipped $221,000 worth of gypsum last year out of this country in the raw state, and we brought back $75,000 worth of-not gypsum-but of plaster of Paris, which is gypsum under another name. That tells vou the whole story. Then, if you read the 'Mineral Industry,' published in the United States-if the House requires I will send to the library and get a copy-you will find that they have great hopes of the gypsum industry in the United States, because the Payne tariff had reduced the duty, and they hoped to get gypsum from Canada. And they expected to be able to mine it cheap, because they could employ labour in these mining operations at $1.20 and $1.35 a day -that is what they wanted to pay our men for mining. I give these figures in the hope that the miners and labourers in Cobalt will read them.
Now. we come to asbestos, another item we are going to be given the privilege of sending free into the United States-a most marvellous thing, that the United States will allow our asbestos to go in free. As a matter of fact, statistics show that 85 per cent-80 per cent at the very least-of all the asbestos of the whole world is produced in Canada. The figures also show that 95 per cent .of the asbestos consumed in the United States is brought into that country from Canada, The Minister of Mines (Mr. Templeman) is in his seat, and I. will ask him to correct me if it is not so.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: He does not know.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Then, again, I have to fall back on myself as an authority.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: What would you do with it?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
We have an absolute monopoly of asbestos-and the great thing has been accomplished of getting asbestos into the United States free. And the minister asks me: ' What would you do with it?' What would I do with it? I would try to manufacture it. Let me tell the minister exactly all about that: If you look through this treaty you will find that a long, lean, dark, hairy hand has manipulated every part of it. I wonder whose it is. Let me put the House onto it. You find its work in the pulp schedule, but not in that schedule alone. Sixty per cent of the asbestos that goes into the United

(States goes to be manufactured into paper. The Minister of Mines asks me what I would do. I would say to the Americans: Gentlemen, there is going to be an export duty on asbestos, and if people want asbestos paper to line their walls, or put under their floors to make their houses fireproof so that they can save one-half of one per cent on their insurance, they will have to come to Canada to get it, and if they want to tax themselves 50 per cent on the import, why, they will add just that much more to the cost; that would be the effect under the economic law which everybody knows and which even Adam Smith himself, strange to say, acknowledges.
And then there is the talc industry. The hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) is not in his place. He was asked what talcum was used for. He sits at the receipt of custom, he knows what goes in and what goes out, what everything is used for and what duty it ought to pay. He said that he understood that talcum was used for 'dressing for the person.' I do not need to turn up ' Hansard ' tci verify that-fortunately my memory is pretty good; I do not think the minister would deny what I have said, even if he were here. I find that they have talcum mines in the United States.' They have very large mines of this material in the state of New York, one in Michigan and Texas, and others in other states of the Union. And the funniest thing about these talcum mines in the United States is that they are all controlled by one corporation. What corporation? The American Paper Company. What do they use talc for? The Minister of Customs evidently did not know, for the talcum used to make what he sees advertised on the blind walls- ' Jones's Borated Talcum Powder '-is all imported from Italy; there is nothing on this continent that is fine enough and white enough for this purpose. That talcum is worth $60 a ton, ours $3.50.
The American Paper Company makes asbestos roofing paper. That great American paper trust figures there again. So in respect to all these minerals that are going to make us all happy, all these great industries in which our workingmen are allowed to make $1 a day and board themselves in mining, they are all really controlled by one great trust on the other side of the line. How much do you think Canada is going to get out of it? I agree with the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Poster), that this policy, in spite of anything that is said by the Prime Minister, is going to be a disastrous one. He tried to teach the chairman of the Conservation Commission his duty, and what a foolish and silly way he used in trying to teach him. He said his business of Chairman of the Committee on Conservation was political science, but that the things we discussed in this House pertained to political economy.
Now I have a recollection of reading in books that nobody has yet decided whether political economy is a science or not, and I would like the right hon. gentleman to explain, if he were present, the difference between political science and political economy.
Well, we all know that the true policy of this country is not to allow anything to go out of the country that is not manufactured, when it can be manufactured in this country, more especially those articles of which we possess an absolute monopoly. We have virtually a monopoly in fish, and still this government invites all the nations of the earth to come in here and fish, to deplete our fishing waters, and destroy this great article of commerce in order that we may worship at the altar of some free trade fetish. We have a monopoly of all the asbestos in the world, but it is going to be sent out of this country, and none of our young men are to be trained to grind that stuff up and manufacture it into paper. The same with gypsum, that also is to be taken away from us; so with our salt mines, they are to be closed down although we had hopes of a great industry from the by-products of salt, and all that will be left for us are the by-products of the salt. We are to be allowed to send away the raw materials for the benefit of the foreigner. The right hon. gentleman said that his ancestors came to this country and dispossessed the Indians of their lands, that the Indians were the true conservators of the land, and the settlers were those who noshed to use them. He drew the analogy to represent our conservation idea, as opposed to his pro-American idea. Now let us follow the analogy out. We are to be the Indians, and we are to be treated as savages and barbarians, and allow those gentlemen to the south to come in here and take away our raw materials, to take them over to the United States and manufacture them. If that is the policy, then I say what is the use of encouraging our young men to study engineering science in order that they may oversee the development of our industries? What is the use of McGill? Why is there a technical school in Nova Scotia? Why is there a technical school in New Brunswick? What is the use of Laval and McGill, with their hundreds and thousands of young men studying technical science in order to become engineers? Yes, and what is the use of our Toronto university, which has the greatest number of young men attending scientific classes of any school in the world, except one, that is the scientific institute in Glasgow? What is the ambition of these young men? They live in hope of achieving the scientific knowledge which will make them leaders in the industries of this country, enable them to superintend the

poor foreigners who come here to use the pick and shovel, building our railroads and developing our natural resources. I say if this policy is to be carried out, then shut the doors of all these scientific schools, throw the keys into the sea, and let all these young men go back to the woods and prepare to handle the pick and the shovel themselves. That is the way this policy impresses itself on my mind. There is nothing in it for this country, either for the present or for the future.
Now let us come to the province of Quebec. Great stress has been laid on the fact that the people of Quebec can export their hay. Well, now, in regard to hay, I have a distinct recollection of reading in some musty text book of English law that in the old country for many years no leases were made unless they contained a clause forbidding the tenant to take a pound of hay or a pound of straw off the land. Hon. gentlemen here who are members of the legal profession will tell you that the same thing obtains in the province of Ontario, where the tenant is not allowed to take a pound of straw or a pound of hay off the farm. Quebec has a great future before it as a farming country, it has a tremendous future before it as a manufacturing country. It has resources of cheap power much greater even than that of the great province of Ontario from which I come. It has a skilful class of people; no people in the world are so deft with their fingers, or so skilful in handling machinery, so quick to learn, so studious and faithful, as the men of Quebec. The forest from which they used to get their livelihood is Tetreating farther and farther back, and little villages are deserted for six months in the year while the fathers and sons leave their homes in order to work in the forest. Would it. not be the proper policy to encourage industries for these villages so the people would not have to leave their homes for employment.
And let me point out that another question arises here. I have shown that the men who organized confederation did it with a set purpose, which purpose is the very antithesis of the policy which underlies this reciprocity treaty. I say that so far as I am concerned, I have not lost faith yet in confederation. Men who have lived in Canada for forty years find that the constitution under which thej' are living is becoming more and more dear to them. There seems to be something in it which touches our hearts. It meets every varying condition of our life, it deals fairly and squarely with all classes. Whilst we may grumble once in a while, I do not think there is anybody who could draw up a better constitution than that which was drafted by the fathers of confederation. Under that constitution certain privileges were justly granted to the French Canad-Mr. CURRIE (Simcoe).
ians, their language and their religion, the same as certain other privileges w.ere granted to the people in my province, and to other provinces. Now, Sir, I assert that confederation is directly challenged by this reciprocity agreement, it is the first great challenge confederation has received since it was consummated.
I would ask these men from Quebec if there is analogy, if there is anything to show them what would happen to them if confederation is set aside. I say yes there is. At one time the state of Louisiana belonged to France. It was sold by Napoleon to the United States. It contained a population exactly of the same race and of the same people as the French Canadians. They spoke the same language, they observed the same doctrine and had the same rights and the same social customs, and they bore about the same proportion relatively to the population of the United States as the present population of Quebec would bear to the population of the United States if Canada were annexed. What has happened to Louisiana? Why, Sir, you can go on the streets of English Toronto and you will hear more French spoken than you will hear on the streets of New Orleans. What has happened to those parish churches built by the fathers ? The Yankees in the south used those old churches for what purpose? To search their registers so that if a man with French Canadian blood attempts to rise in politics or otherwise, if they can find from the register that there is a drop of black blood in an ancestor, ten or twelve generations back, the man is put into a Jim Crow car. Many of these French Canadians came from Demerara, Martinique and Dominica, and to-day every one with a French name who cannot show a clean bill of health is under suspicion as to nis colour and we all know how strong the colour feeling is in the south. It would be the same here. If a French Canadian who voted for this agreement, bartering away the rights of confederation for a bale of hay, asked me to vote for him and I were a French Canadian, I would say, if you think that I would vote for you after you have done that, you must think I am only fit to don a pair of long ears and eat a bale of hay.
Now we come to the great province of Ontario. That province can pretty .nearly take care of itself so far as any Americans are concerned. We are not afraid of them, we will welcome them, we will take them in on any deal from a game of poker up. Some of our best men from the province of Ontario are building their great railways. Jim Hill, who is from Ontario, taught them how to build railways, and he was the first man who taught the United States

managers how to manage railways, the first to teach them railway statistics. I could point to other eminent men in the United States from my province. This arrangement touches my province closely. The one thing about the treaty is that there is not a single word from end to end as regards the working men. That is a serious thing. We will take one class, the truck gardeners. Possibly there may be other gentlemen in the House who can deal with that better than I can, but having lived in the south of the United States for a while, and knowing the conditions, perhaps I may be pardoned if I enlarge a trifle on it. Many people have asked why the Ontario intensive farmers or truck gardeners are opposed to this arrangement. They say that our truck gardeners can grow stuff as cheaply as in the United States. On its face that seems a plausible argument, but let us examine it. The man in the south, in Florida, starts growing his truck in January. He does not have to pay any big money for a house for himself and family. I have ridden along in the Southern States and counted the pickaninnies through the chinks in the logs. He has not to buy expensive clothing, he has not to sit in the house for six months while the soil is covered with snow, and he has nqt to buy coal. He starts things growing on his truck farm early in January and he can get coloured help, men, women and children at fifty cents a day or less. They grow their truck in every month in the year, they get three or four crops a year, because there is no snow, and the conditions . for growth are ideal. You ask me, can a man in Ontario do that. The grower in the south does not have to pay for glass or hotbeds or steam, but the man in Ontario has, and the only profit which the Ontario man makes is the little profit off the first three or four weeks of the early crop; the rest of the time he is simply turning his crop over and perhaps paying expenses. You take away his little profit, his means of livelihood. I have had to make my livelihood and I know what touches the heart of every worker; and the man who has worked for hire, when he sees one of his fellows injured, says: That injury is to me also-and that is why Ontario is against this agreement. If it hurt only that one class of man, every worker in my province in his heart feels sore. He would say: Why should we injure these men and deprive them of their livelihood? It may be my turn next. We have not heard any promise here to-day that it would not be our turn next. We were told by the right hon. gentleman who leads this government that these ambassadors had not gone as far in the way of taking duties off manufactured goods as
he might have gone. That, I take it, is a plain intimation of what he may do if he had another chance at it. We have heard a great deal about transportation systems. We have two roads that can take care of themselves. Who is going to be hurt? Not the two big railway companies, because the two chief men have said that they will take care of themselves and no doubt they can, they have the money and resources, they are building lines to Duluth to-day, endeavouring to meet this crisis. It is the thousands of men employed on the railways of Canada who are now deriving a living from this traffic who will be hurt; they will be deprived of their labour, they will have to sell their houses for nothing and leave the country and go to the United States if this traffic goes to the United States, as it will, because, as I have shown, the moment a treaty of this kind comes into effect, 50 per cent of our traffic will go south of the St. Lawrence. It was so before, it will be so again. As I said, there is nothing in this for the working man, who sees his fellow touched all along; he is told this is going to make the prices higher for the farmer, but that means that living will cost more to him. He will not get more wages, because his wages are dependent not on protection or free trade to any large extent, but largely upon the situation of the labour market itself. I have said that the livelihood of these men will be taken away. The moment the labour of a man in Ontario is displaced by that of a man in the United States we initiate a period of hard times. If you take away a quarter of the work given in a factory in Canada and give it to the United States you may not hurt the man who owns the factory but you hurt one-quarter of the workmen, and they are the people who are the ultimate sufferers. That is the secret of the whole thing.
We hear a great deal about the cattle trade in Ontario. The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) told the House with a great deal of chest beating, that he would warrant that the statistics of the ' Mail ' were very reliable, and that if one opened the ' Mail ' he would find that at any time in the last ten years the price of beef cattle was higher in Chicago than in Toronto.
That seemed strange to me, because when I wras a young newspaper man I used to write the market reports for the ' Mail,' and I knew a little about the business. However, I went to the library and I hunted up the files of the ' Mail,' and I took the prices at haphazard during May in these several years, and I have prepared a table, and that table shows among other things that when a profes-

The facts with regard to our production of barley were set out very clearly by the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro), but I would emphasize that the barley quotations given in the United States newspapers are for what is known as malting barley, which grades No. 1, while out of the three or four million bushels of barley grown in the northwest and Ontario over 90 per cent of it does not grade up to No. 3, and there is the additional fact that if the barley is fed to hogs and cattle it is worth one dollar per bushel to-day under any condition of market, as compared with 85 cents paid in the United States for malting barley. Now, this treaty will be -a serious injury to -the horse trade in Ontario, which does a very large trade in .horses with the northwest. The best explanation of the injurious effect of the treaty op the horse business comes to me from a gentleman who is not exactly a dealer, but who (as did his father before him) has done more to improve horse breeding in the province of Ontario than any man I know of; I refer to Major Wm. Hendrie, of Hamilton, who, when he learned about this reciprocity treaty, sent me a note, in which he says:
Free entry of horses into our Northwest will put horse breeding back 20 years and will destroy that market for the Ontario farmer.
That is what Major Hendrie has to say about it and he has put the whole thing in a nutshell. A word about the effect of this treaty on our transportation interests and especially with reference to the carriage of freight on the Great Lakes. Anybody who knows anything about the Great Lakes traffic knows that 15 years ago our freight carriers on the Great Lakes consisted of a few wooden scows of the type of Dr. Drummond's ' Julie Plante.' To-day we have over 70 fine steel vessels engaged in that traffic, none of them less than 2,000 _ tons capacity, and probably 20 of them built in Great Lake ports, where employment is afforded every day in the year for 1,200 men. That traffic has grown and increased enormously, until now it is estimated that there are over 5,000 men employed on these boats, and from 12,000 to 15,000 men em-

ployed in the trade altogether, from stevedores to captains. The Minister of Customs pointed out that a certain amount of grain automatically found its way to Buffalo at any rate, and asked: ' What does that mean? It does not mean that there is going to be anything to hurt thi§ trade.' But I notice that while there is reciprocity in agricultural products in this treaty, there is not reciprocity in the coasting laws which are in force on the Great Lakes, and once the grain goes south of the line before it reaches Fort William, a Canadian vessel will not get a pound of that freight, but it will go to Chicago or Buffalo, and most of it will be ground into flour. It will act simply as a displacement, that is to say, you will put in so much Canadian wheat at one end and they will send out so much American wheat at the other end. The Americans will use our wheat simply to improve their grades, and they will benefit by it. They will benefit to the tune of exactly $30 a car on every carload of our grain that they take their way, because the only places where they grow No. 1 hard is in Dakota and in other states bordering on Canada, and as these states do not supply the whole market they have a monopoly, which enables them to raise the price above that of our No. 1 Northern in Manitoba. But No. 1 Manitoba wheat is superior to any other class of wheat in America, and the moment we give the Americans access to our market. No. 1 Manitoba wheat will come down to the price of ordinary American wheat, and will not grade higher. At the same time, the moment this treaty goes into force one-half the St. Lawrence trade will be cut off and we will not have one-half the ships built in our shipyards that we have now, and that is something which affects me very seriously. We all hoped to see the shipbuilding industry grow up on all our coasts, but this treaty will prove to be a great disaster to that industry. You might as well dump the elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur into Lake Superior, because our grain, instead of going to these ports, will find its competitive point at Duluth, .and the elevators there will get all the benefit of it, and if it can be shipped via Duluth without having to be bonded, the shippers are not going to ship it by Fort William or Port Arthur when they can ship it by a route 70 miles shorter. That is what is going to happen to that traffic.

Our domestic markets and trade are therefore, worth to us ten times as much as our trade with the United States.
The dollar in domestic trade is exchanged ten times oftener.
Why then are we so anxious to get another market when we have now a market worth ten times as much. Adam Smith said in his ' Wealth of Nations,' that a pound in domestic trade was turned over twenty-four times as often as a pound in foreign trade, so that it makes a profit that many times more employed at home than employed abroad. In his day of sailing ships domestic trade, he said, was twenty-four times as much exchanged as foreign trade, but with

the fast steamships and railways of to-day the comparison of the trade is reduced, as I have shown in this table, from 24 to 10. I have shown you clearly that the difference in favour of the home trade is as ten to one. That is to say for every dollar you put into the home trade, it turns over ten times faster than if put it into trade with the United States. Consequently it would be far better for us to increase and foster our trade at home than to seek foreign markets.	.
If I desired to follow this question longer, I could show you how every country in the world tried protection before Great Britain did. Adam Smith and the anti-protectionists wrote, towards the close of the Eighteenth century, and their doctrines were promulgated throughout all the countries of Europe, and free trade was ajdopted and tried by every other country long before Great Britain adopted it.
It was not until 1847, as I have already told you, that they adopted free trade, and they did not adopt it on many manufactures until years afterwards. They always wanted other countries to give them free trade; and as soon as they got free trade in those countries, they stole their markets and took away their business. They did that with Portugal, by what is known as the Methuen treaty. They offered Portugal free admission for its wine in consideration of free admission of British woollens and other goods. Portugal at that time, had a magnificent trade with hex colonies, almost as great as that of Great Britain. Great Britain seized this- trade, and not only that, but took away the accumulated gold of Portugal. She bought silks in India and China and sold them in Germany, where they had1 free trade and put the silk trade of Germany and France out of business, bringing immense profits, into England. They are pretty keen traders.
To-day you will find that every country in the world has repudiated free trade. Except Great Britain and Turkey. What is the use of any one trying to deny that land to make pretension of being a free trader? If you axe a free trader, you must be a cosmopolitan one, who believes that his own country should throw out lifelines to every other country in the world. But if you are a nationalist in tariff matters, you want to help your own country first. And, so far as this country is concerned, I believe it is better for us to be more nationalist. Did I desire to take up the time of the House, I could give quotations of figures for different countries of the world when they had free trade and when they had protection. I could give figures comparing wages in England with wages in the United States and Canada. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) said that
wages_ were as good or better in England than in any other country, except the United States. I grant you that the trade unions have made wages good in the old country. But the real test of a nation's greatness in industrial progress is the test of unemployment, and England has a greater percentage of unemployed than any other country in the world. There is only one other country that can rank with England in regard to pauperism, and that also is a free trade country-Turkey. When you findthatfrom twfenty-seven to thirty persons out of a thousand in England are receiving charity, in order that they may live and not starve, you find a condition of things which we here wish to avoid. We want to grow up and be left alone, and to develop our own resources along the old line of confederation. The best analogy that I have ever seen given of an industrial nation is a hive of bees. Protect the bees, give them a good hive, and they will look after themselves; they will thrive and lay up plenty of honey and will live through the winter and do their work perfectly. But allow some one to come along and knock a few slats off the hive and what happens? You have a disturbance, and in a few days after free trade has been established with other bees, you have a raid on that hive and the honey is stolen. And that is- what will occur in this case. We are getting along very nicely. We had our own walls up and the slats of our hive nailed down tight-. We were doing business along our own lines and were learning every day how to do it better. Why, we were learning more political economy in a few yeays than Adam Smith and all these other fellows eveT thought about. You could go to one end of our country and find there the hunter, the earliest economic producer. You could find! the hunter giving place to the herdsman, the herdsman giving place to the man who wanted to till the whole earth, the extensive farmer, and you could find the extensive farmer giving place to the intensive farmer. These oldi professors in the old country who wrote about political economy told about something like this that they thought had occurred three or four hundred years before. Why, we saw these things going on right under our own eyes. We learned, for instance, the lesson of land values as they never could learn it. We have seen western towns grow in a few years from little collections of shacks to great cities. We have learned banking in the same way. We have made the mistakes that led to busted banks, and we have seen them bust. We have learned about wages;- we have learned all these elements of political economy by hard practical experience. And when you come down to hard fact,

there is not an educated farmer in Canada, but knows more about practical economy, its facts and its laws, than all the writers that ever came out of Manchester and all the soap box orators that ever came out of Hyde Park. Why, it makes me feel cold to hear these men who have come here preaching to us what we ought to do. It is much the same as if a mandarin from the paddy fields of his native China, were to come over here with his button cap, go into a harvest field in the Northwest, and tell the farmer how to run his reaper; or as if a school teacher who had been instructing a class in physics five hundred miles from the sea, were to go down to an ocean port, go aboard a ship like the Mauretania, and undertake to instruct the chief engineer how to run his engines. These men come over here and from organizations of every kind, and start shouting. In some places they talk on the street corners-and the policeman comes 'and gently moves them on. But after a while the good wages they get have an effect on them. They become contented, and when they do, they make the best citizens. But I am afraid that in the Northwest the climate has not agreed with some of them, and they have formed organizations there and are trying to show the good old farmer from Ontario how to manage their own affairs and how to be economical.
Let me say to the right lion, gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) who leads this House: After all, the one great thing on trial here, is not so much this trade -arrangement as the great compact made between the various portions of the country. Confederation itself is on trial. We have to decide whether we will vote confidence in the constitution that was -adopted so many years ago or whether we will vote want of confidence. For my part, I am going to vote confidence in it, and I think the bulk of the men of all parties in this country, whether Liberals or Conservatives, will hack up -that old historical party that has always stood for the Canadian idea; and, when the day comes to decide on this question -at the ballot box, you will find these men voting this government -out of office, and you will hear no more of this reciprocity for the next hundred and fifty years.

I trust my hon. friend from North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) will not deem it discourteous of me, if I do not attempt to follow him in his very interesting and very discursive address. That address contained many statements that would require correction, many that would require further illustration and explanation; but if I were to attempt to deal with the hon. gentleman's Mr. CURRIE (Simcoe).
argument and -also to refer to the question with which I wish to deal. I should be compelled to go far beyond the limited time for which I -desire to ask the attention of the committee and. would need to take up as much time, as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Currie, Simcoe) himself, has occupied.
* My purpose in speaking on this question at this time is to direct the attention of the committee to the attitude of the province from which I come towards the trade arrangement that has been made between Canada and the United States. I also desire to point out what, in my opinion, will be the effect on the trade of British Columbia when that trade arrangement goes into force. Many of the speeches which have thus far been delivered by hon. gentlemen opposite have been confined almost exclusively to the denunciation of the agreement because its effect has been to remove customs taxation. They have argued that the effects of this agreement would impair the loyalty of Canadians, that it would cause a deflection of trade from east and west to north and south, and ultimately lead to the annexation of Canada with the United States. Now from the standpoint of the province of British Columbia, I can assure this Ho-use that the -loyalty of our people does not depend upon commercial relations with the United States. Long before confederation, and after confederation, there was in British Columbia a very extensive trade from north to south, there was no trade whatever from east to west. During the old days there was absolutely no trade east and west, but all the trade of British Columbia was transacted with the state of California. Yet the pioneers of that day did not waver in their allegiance to the British Crown, they were quite as loyal then as they are now. The argument that Canadian allegiance and Canadian aspirations of nationhood under the old flag are such fickle things that they must be kept in the straight and narrow path by the imposition of penalties in the shape of trade restrictions, does not seem to me to be one that will meet with the approval of this House, or of the public opinion of Canada. That argument, or something of a similar character, has been made to do duty in Canada for as long as I can remember. The argument has been used for the purpose of discrediting the Liberal party, for purely party political purposes, but always unsuccessfully, as I am sure it will be on the present occasion.
In confining my remarks therefore to the consideration of the question how this agreement will affect British Columbia, I do not ignore the vaster question of how it will affect all Canada. I simply prefer dealing with one phase of a many-sided question, a phase also which I think is of sufficient importance to merit a little special consideration at my hands. After a

careful study of the opinion of British Columbia, as expressed by the press of that province, by public meetings, by letters and telegrams received, I am as confident as one can be that the consensus of opinion in British Columbia is that this agreement is a good thing, that as a business proposition it will be advantageous to that province, that it will accelerate the development of British Columbia, and add very greatly and rapidly to its population. I wish to indicate the opinion of British Columbia in respect to the effect this trade agreement will have on the fruit industry. My hon. friend the member for Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell) delivered a very long and interesting speech a few days ago, in which he dwelt altogether upon the effect of this agreement upon the fruit industry of British Columbia. He placed on ' Hansard ' a number of strong petitions from boards of trade, from members of fruit associations and others, and I believe the member for New Westminster (Mr. Taylor) also read several warm protests against the agreement. Now I have in my hand a large number of opinions from prominent men. 1 will not read them all, but I desire to give the names of those who sent them and the purport of what they say. I think it is important that the House should know that, even in the great fruit growing district of Okanagan, the opinion is not unanimously opposed to this agreement; I rather think that the majority even of the people of the Okanagan country will be found favourable to the ratification of the agreement. I will briefly state the results as I have them. I have in my hand a telegram from the Nelson Liberal Association.
